pathway.title: FAIR ISAAC CORP — Credit Snapshot
pathway.question: Should we own this issuer, in which instrument, and why?

runs.text: The most important finding is that leverage is now set by shareholder-return policy rather than by operations. CP-1 shows total debt up from US$3,055.7m to US$5,582.4m over nine months and nine-month cash repurchases of US$3,046.0m against free cash flow of US$750.0m; the business context shows the term loan proceeds were used to fund an accelerated share repurchase and that a $2.0 billion repurchase authorisation is in place. The mechanism is direct: each repurchase round is financed by borrowing, so analyst total debt to EBITDA of 4.46x can rise or fall by board decision alone. The implication is that the creditor's leverage tolerance depends on a choice nobody has committed to constrain, other than the financial covenant.

The second finding is the covenant path. The stated maximum consolidated leverage ratio is 4.5x until December 30, 2026, 4.0x from December 31, 2026 and 3.5x from December 31, 2027. On the analyst measure of operating income plus depreciation and amortisation, total debt to EBITDA is 4.46x, which leaves a cushion of 0.95% of EBITDA below 4.5x (Calculations); on the sensitivity with share-based compensation added back it is 3.91x. The covenant definition is not supplied, so neither is the covenant ratio, and the compliance statement in the filings is the only evidence of headroom. The step down to 4.0x on December 31, 2026 requires EBITDA growth, debt reduction or a favourable definition; the quarterly term loan instalments and free cash flow provide the repayment capacity.

The third finding is interest burden. Cash interest paid in the last twelve months is US$164.9m but annualised contractual interest on June 30, 2026 balances is US$316.5m, because the term loan was drawn on June 5, 2026 and the 2026 notes in March 2026. Cover is 7.60x as reported and 3.96x on the run-rate. About US$2,210.0m of borrowings float over SOFR, so base rates feed straight into the burden.

The fourth finding is revenue concentration. Three consumer reporting agencies produced 63% of revenue in the June 2026 quarter, and Scores growth was primarily attributed to a higher mortgage origination scores unit price. The mechanism is that a per-score fee through three intermediaries, a regulated mortgage channel and a single price lever determine most of earnings and almost all of the incremental margin, given a Scores margin of 91%. A pricing, volume or policy change therefore hits EBITDA, interest cover and covenant headroom together.

The fifth finding is liquidity and maturities. Cash is US$248.4m, the derived undrawn revolver is US$290.0m before letters of credit, and US$300.0m of term loan amortisation falls due within twelve months, against last twelve months free cash flow of US$960.9m. The maturity profile is back-ended into FY2028, when US$1,987.5m falls due. The implication is that near-term liquidity is sufficient but refinancing will need market access at higher coupons, since the 2026 notes carry 6.25% against 5.25% on the repaid notes.

runs.text: Strengths. First, earnings power: segment margins are very high and Scores generates a 91% operating margin, so operating income of US$1,236.3m for the last twelve months converts into analyst EBITDA of US$1,252.4m on light capital spending; the mechanism is low incremental cost, which supports debt service. Second, cash conversion: free cash flow of US$960.9m for the last twelve months and US$750.0m for nine months, supported by billing in advance, means scheduled amortisation is covered by internal cash. Third, recurring visibility in Software: annual recurring revenue of US$815.8m and net retention of 109%, with platform retention well above 100%, supports a base of contracted revenue, though it is the smaller segment. Fourth, discretionary use of cash: because the leverage increase came from repurchases, not from a structural commitment, the board can slow repurchases to reduce debt; the revolver extends to 2030 and the term loan amortises. Fifth, simple structure: the debt is unsecured, with no sponsor, and no priming, drop-down or non-pro-rata exchange is documented, though the absence of such terms in executed documents is not established.

Weaknesses. First, leverage and covenant path: 4.46x on the analyst measure against a 4.5x maximum that steps to 4.0x and 3.5x; the mechanism is shrinking permitted leverage unless EBITDA grows or debt is repaid. Second, financial policy: debt-funded distributions of US$3,046.0m for nine months against free cash flow of US$750.0m, with a stockholders' deficit that carries no equity cushion. Third, concentration: bureaus at 63% of revenue, financial services at 92% and the Americas at 87% of FY2025 revenue, and mortgage-policy exposure. Fourth, interest burden: run-rate interest of US$316.5m is nearly double last twelve months cash interest, with floating-rate exposure. Fifth, disclosure limits: no company EBITDA, no covenant ratio, no executed documents, no proxy statement, no data after July 29, 2026; these restrict monitoring more than they signal risk, and missing evidence is not treated as adverse.

runs.text: There is no sponsor transaction, merger or acquisition in the supplied sources; the context lists no deal terms. The transactions that matter to a creditor are the issuer's own financing and capital return events in fiscal 2026. On March 20, 2026 the company issued senior notes carrying a 6.25% coupon and maturing September 15, 2034, in a private offering to qualified institutional investors, and on March 26, 2026 it used the proceeds to repay in full the 2018 Senior Notes before their May 2026 maturity (10-Q page:12). On June 5, 2026 it amended its credit agreement to provide a term loan borrowed in full that day and maturing May 15, 2028, with quarterly amortisation, and the 10-Q states that the proceeds were used to fund an accelerated share repurchase agreement (10-Q page:11, page:22). The same day it entered an accelerated share repurchase agreement with Wells Fargo Securities, paying $1.5 billion and receiving an initial delivery of shares equal to approximately 80 percent of the expected total, with $300.0 million treated as a prepayment pending settlement, which the company expects in the fourth quarter of fiscal 2026 (10-Q page:13). The June 2026 repurchase program authorises repurchases up to an aggregate cost of $2.0 billion, of which $800.0 million remained at June 30, 2026, including the prepayment awaiting settlement (10-Q page:36). In sum, the financing replaced a maturing note with a longer note and added a term loan whose proceeds were returned to shareholders, taking total debt from US$3,055.7m at September 30, 2025 to US$5,582.4m at June 30, 2026 per the financial base. Liquidity effect: cash is US$248.4m and the derived undrawn revolver is US$290.0m before letters of credit, and the term loan amortises at a quarterly rate with US$300.0m due within twelve months. The status of each event is completed except the settlement of the repurchase agreement, which is a stated expectation, and the September 30, 2026 instalment and later events are Not supplied because nothing after the July 29, 2026 filings is in the pack. The credit agreement, its June 5, 2026 amendment, the indenture for the 2026 notes and the repurchase agreement are not supplied, so the amortisation schedule, guarantor position, covenant definitions and any restrictions on distributions rest on the 10-Q summary text. The use of proceeds and debt raised are Documentary Facts; the characterisation of the repurchase as returning capital to stockholders is Management Language (10-K page:63).

fields.value: FICO's operations generate strong, growing cash flow, but the June 30, 2026 balance sheet is a different credit from the one at FY2025. In nine months, with total debt rising by US$2,526.7m, the company drew a new US$1,500.0m term loan, issued US$1,000.0m of 2034 notes, repaid the US$400.0m 2018 notes and borrowed further on the revolver, taking total debt from US$3,055.7m to US$5,582.4m. The proceeds funded US$3,046.0m of share repurchases, including a US$1,500.0m accelerated share repurchase, far above free cash flow. On an analyst EBITDA of operating income plus depreciation and amortisation, total debt to EBITDA moved from 3.25x to 4.46x, and cash interest cover from 9.07x to 7.60x on a lagging cash-paid basis. Interest on the new debt is only partly in the last twelve months, so the run-rate burden is materially higher than reported cash interest. The main limits are the absence of a company-defined EBITDA or covenant ratio, the absence of the credit agreement, and the absence of anything after the July 29, 2026 filings. fields.value: FICO is a Delaware-incorporated, NYSE-listed analytics company with two segments. Scores sells the FICO Score mainly through Experian, TransUnion and Equifax, which pay FICO a fee for each score generated; Software sells decisioning products as SaaS or on-premises. Revenue is concentrated by counterparty (three bureaus), by end market (financial services) and by geography (the Americas), and recent growth is concentrated in Scores pricing on mortgage originations. The company has no sponsor and no controlling holder is evidenced in the supplied sources; ownership detail sits in a proxy statement that is not supplied. The creditor-relevant change in the period is financial policy: in FY2026 the company issued new notes, drew a term loan and funded a large accelerated share repurchase, taking analyst total debt to EBITDA to 4.46x per the financial base. The documented behaviour is debt-funded shareholder distribution within the permissions of an unsecured credit agreement and in compliance with its stated covenants; no priming, drop-down or non-pro-rata exchange is documented. The business is high-margin and cash generative, but its revenue depends on a small number of counterparties and on score pricing, so the credit rests on continued pricing power and on management's leverage choices, not on structural protection.

The same day it entered an accelerated share repurchase agreement with Wells Fargo Securities, paying $1.5 billion and receiving an initial delivery of shares equal to approximately 80 percent of the expected total, with $300.0 million treated as a prepayment pending settlement, which the company expects in the fourth quarter of fiscal 2026 (10-Q page:13). The June 2026 repurchase program authorises repurchases up to an aggregate cost of $2.0 billion, of which $800.0 million remained at June 30, 2026, including the prepayment awaiting settlement (10-Q page:36). In sum, the financing replaced a maturing note with a longer note and added a term loan whose proceeds were returned to shareholders, taking total debt from US$3,055.7m at September 30, 2025 to US$5,582.4m at June 30, 2026 per the financial base. fields.name: Quote
fields.value: FICO's business risk is strong on earnings quality but narrow on sources: a per-score fee model with very high segment margins, recurring Software revenue with net retention above 100%, light capital spending and consistent free cash flow. Its financial risk has moved sharply in fiscal 2026. Total debt rose from US$3,055.7m to US$5,582.4m while cash repurchases of US$3,046.0m for nine months far exceeded free cash flow of US$750.0m, and analyst total debt to EBITDA rose from 3.25x at FY2025 to 4.46x at June 30, 2026, which is 4.26x net. The stated covenant maximum is 4.5x until December 30, 2026, then 4.0x, then 3.5x, and on the analyst measure the cushion below 4.5x is thin; on a sensitivity that adds back share-based compensation the ratio is 3.91x. The covenant definition is not supplied, so headroom is Not calculable. Interest on the June 2026 debt is only partly in reported cash interest, so run-rate cover is about 3.96x against 7.60x reported. Liquidity is adequate for the near term but not generous: cash of US$248.4m plus a derived undrawn revolver of US$290.0m, against US$300.0m of term loan amortisation due within twelve months, which free cash flow comfortably covers. The next refinancing step is large: US$1,987.5m falls due in FY2028, when the term loan balance and the 2019 and 2021 notes mature. Because the debt is unsecured and no creditor-adverse action is documented, the creditor relies on covenants, cash generation and the board's financial policy, not on collateral or a sponsor. Overall the fundamental credit view is a high-quality earnings stream carrying a materially higher and still discretionary debt load; confidence is medium because covenant definitions, ownership detail and everything after July 29, 2026 are Not supplied.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: The most important finding is that leverage is now set by shareholder-return policy rather than by operations. CP-1 shows total debt up from US$3,055.7m to US$5,582.4m over nine months and nine-month cash repurchases of US$3,046.0m against free cash flow of US$750.0m; the business context shows the term loan proceeds were used to fund an accelerated share repurchase and that a $2.0 billion repurchase authorisation is in place. The mechanism is direct: each repurchase round is financed by borrowing, so analyst total debt to EBITDA of 4.46x can rise or fall by board decision alone. The implication is that the creditor's leverage tolerance depends on a choice nobody has committed to constrain, other than the financial covenant.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: The second finding is the covenant path. The stated maximum consolidated leverage ratio is 4.5x until December 30, 2026, 4.0x from December 31, 2026 and 3.5x from December 31, 2027. On the analyst measure of operating income plus depreciation and amortisation, total debt to EBITDA is 4.46x, which leaves a cushion of 0.95% of EBITDA below 4.5x (Calculations); on the sensitivity with share-based compensation added back it is 3.91x. The covenant definition is not supplied, so neither is the covenant ratio, and the compliance statement in the filings is the only evidence of headroom. The step down to 4.0x on December 31, 2026 requires EBITDA growth, debt reduction or a favourable definition; the quarterly term loan instalments and free cash flow provide the repayment capacity.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: The third finding is interest burden. Cash interest paid in the last twelve months is US$164.9m but annualised contractual interest on June 30, 2026 balances is US$316.5m, because the term loan was drawn on June 5, 2026 and the 2026 notes in March 2026. Cover is 7.60x as reported and 3.96x on the run-rate. About US$2,210.0m of borrowings float over SOFR, so base rates feed straight into the burden.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: The fourth finding is revenue concentration. Three consumer reporting agencies produced 63% of revenue in the June 2026 quarter, and Scores growth was primarily attributed to a higher mortgage origination scores unit price. The mechanism is that a per-score fee through three intermediaries, a regulated mortgage channel and a single price lever determine most of earnings and almost all of the incremental margin, given a Scores margin of 91%. A pricing, volume or policy change therefore hits EBITDA, interest cover and covenant headroom together.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: The fifth finding is liquidity and maturities. Cash is US$248.4m, the derived undrawn revolver is US$290.0m before letters of credit, and US$300.0m of term loan amortisation falls due within twelve months, against last twelve months free cash flow of US$960.9m. The maturity profile is back-ended into FY2028, when US$1,987.5m falls due. The implication is that near-term liquidity is sufficient but refinancing will need market access at higher coupons, since the 2026 notes carry 6.25% against 5.25% on the repaid notes.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Strengths. First, earnings power: segment margins are very high and Scores generates a 91% operating margin, so operating income of US$1,236.3m for the last twelve months converts into analyst EBITDA of US$1,252.4m on light capital spending; the mechanism is low incremental cost, which supports debt service. Second, cash conversion: free cash flow of US$960.9m for the last twelve months and US$750.0m for nine months, supported by billing in advance, means scheduled amortisation is covered by internal cash. Third, recurring visibility in Software: annual recurring revenue of US$815.8m and net retention of 109%, with platform retention well above 100%, supports a base of contracted revenue, though it is the smaller segment. Fourth, discretionary use of cash: because the leverage increase came from repurchases, not from a structural commitment, the board can slow repurchases to reduce debt; the revolver extends to 2030 and the term loan amortises. Fifth, simple structure: the debt is unsecured, with no sponsor, and no priming, drop-down or non-pro-rata exchange is documented, though the absence of such terms in executed documents is not established.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Weaknesses. First, leverage and covenant path: 4.46x on the analyst measure against a 4.5x maximum that steps to 4.0x and 3.5x; the mechanism is shrinking permitted leverage unless EBITDA grows or debt is repaid. Second, financial policy: debt-funded distributions of US$3,046.0m for nine months against free cash flow of US$750.0m, with a stockholders' deficit that carries no equity cushion. Third, concentration: bureaus at 63% of revenue, financial services at 92% and the Americas at 87% of FY2025 revenue, and mortgage-policy exposure. Fourth, interest burden: run-rate interest of US$316.5m is nearly double last twelve months cash interest, with floating-rate exposure. Fifth, disclosure limits: no company EBITDA, no covenant ratio, no executed documents, no proxy statement, no data after July 29, 2026; these restrict monitoring more than they signal risk, and missing evidence is not treated as adverse.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Thesis (one sentence): FICO's very profitable, cash-generative but concentrated Scores franchise supports its debt, while debt-funded buybacks and a stepping-down leverage covenant make the credit depend on pricing power and on the board's financial policy.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: The trace holds. All 29 quotations in the financial base and business context handoffs were found, and each sits on the page it cites. In the readiness handoff every quotation of source text was found; its three other quoted strings are search terms or paraphrases, not source quotations. Every non-derived figure in those handoffs appears in the pinned sources, and every derived figure recomputes from its cited inputs. The four handoffs agree on every shared figure; differences are only the presentation of US$ thousands as US$m. Two qualifications matter for committee use. First, the leverage cushion, the interest run-rate, the undrawn revolver and the maturity schedule are analyst constructions: each is labelled as derived upstream, and each rests on inputs the filings summarise rather than on executed documents. Second, statements about the absence of creditor-adverse terms and about covenant headroom are absence-of-evidence claims and are bounded by the missing credit agreement, indentures and proxy. One wording defect was found in the credit synthesis (a quarter margin stated without its period), recorded below and corrected here. The run supports restricted committee use: permitted for the business description, reported financials, debt structure, liquidity and concentration facts; not permitted for covenant headroom, guarantor or security conclusions, or ownership and related-party conclusions.
